query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying an alumina-based protective coating to steel surfaces will reduce oxidation rates by forming a stable oxide barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: Uncoated steel substrate in air at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Deposition of an Al2O3-containing protective layer (e.g., via thermal spray).
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at 700–900 °C for a prolonged period (e.g., 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense and adherent alumina scale at the substrate–coating interface.
generation.mechanism: The continuous alumina layer acts as a diffusion barrier, slowing oxygen ingress and metal ion outward diffusion, thereby reducing oxide growth.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated substrates exhibit a lower weight gain (e.g., ≥50% reduction) compared to uncoated samples under identical test conditions.
generation.baseline: Oxidation behavior of the uncoated steel substrate under the same temperature and environment.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness may diminish if coating integrity is compromised by mechanical damage or if exposure temperature exceeds coating stability range.
generation.uncertainty: Actual oxidation resistance may vary depending on coating thickness, composition, and deposition parameters; no direct external evidence currently provided.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical sets of steel coupons, apply alumina-based coatings to one set, leave another set uncoated, then subject both to isothermal oxidation at 700–900 °C in air for 100 hours.
measurements: Mass change of samples before and after exposure
Thickness and morphology of oxide scale via cross-sectional analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain or comparable oxide scale thickness reduction, or if the coatings fail to form durable alumina scales, the hypothesis is not supported.
